reason: The warm afternoon sets up the heat response that should lead to sweating.
expectation: The body will experience the warm conditions, setting up a response to heat.

alternatives.reason: The glands produce sweat, but the whole body seems like the starting point for the weather change.

effect: The warming is sensed by the skin and brain, so I can now follow the response toward sweating.
reaction: The signal travelling from skin to brain makes the next step clearer.
reason: Sweat glands are the direct next piece for the goal of cooling through evaporation.
expectation: The warming signal will activate the sweat glands and put sweat on the skin.

alternatives.reason: Skin vessels may also respond to warmth, but the current goal specifically asks about sweat.

effect: The compatibility hint showed that skin vessels respond before the sweat glands; wider vessels bring more blood and heat near the skin.
reaction: I was surprised the vessel response had to come first.
reason: Now that warm blood is flowing near the skin, the sweat glands seem like the next step toward evaporation.
expectation: The sweat glands will produce sweat on the skin.

effect: Sweat has reached the skin, but it still needs to evaporate to carry heat away.
reaction: The distinction between sweating and evaporation is clear now.
reason: Air at the skin is shown carrying water molecules away, matching the evaporation goal.
expectation: Sweat will evaporate into the air and carry heat away from the body.

effect: Evaporation carried heat away, and the new goal shifts to the cold evening.
reaction: It was helpful to see the sweat signal fade as temperature moved back toward its earlier range.
reason: The cold evening is the visible starting point for the new heat-conservation goal.
expectation: The body will sense the colder surroundings and begin a cold response.

effect: The body has sensed the cold and reduced sweating; it still needs to conserve and make heat.
reaction: It makes sense that sweating decreases in the cold.
reason: Skin vessels responded to warmth earlier, so they may also help conserve heat in the cold.
expectation: The skin vessels will narrow, reducing blood flow near the surface and heat loss.

alternatives.reason: Muscle could help make heat, but conserving heat through the skin seems like a useful first step.

effect: Narrower skin vessels reduce heat loss but do not make heat, so the heat-making part remains.
reaction: The distinction between conserving heat and making it is useful.
reason: Skeletal muscle is the remaining visible piece that could help the body make heat.
expectation: The muscles will respond to the cold, possibly by shivering and producing heat.

effect: Shivering completes the cold response: repeated muscle contractions use energy and produce heat, while narrowed skin vessels reduce heat loss.
reaction: Seeing heat conservation and heat production work together was satisfying.

mostWorthwhile.text: Comparing the cold vessel response with shivering was most worthwhile because it showed the difference between holding heat in and making more.

leastWorthwhile.text: The initial warm-up was less engaging because it mainly set up the response rather than showing how the body cooled.

surprise.text: I expected to activate sweat glands immediately, but the game first directed me to the skin vessels. The result showed wider vessels carrying more heat toward the skin.

arbitrary.text: Requiring the skin-vessel response before sweating felt somewhat arbitrary: the result showed what the vessels do, but did not explain why that had to come first.

continue.text: I would choose to continue if another chapter connects familiar body responses this clearly; comparing the warm and cold responses made the choices interesting, though the required order was not always clear.
